 Study finds Minnesota SNAP enrollment barely declines as USDA raises concerns 
 By Elyse Apel | The Center Square 
 Elyse S. Apel 
 Author email

 1 hr ago 
 Facebook 
 Twitter 
 WhatsApp 
 SMS 
 Email

 (The Center Square) – Minnesota saw one of the smallest year-over-year declines in SNAP enrollment nationwide, according to a recently-released study.
 The state also recorded one of the largest year-over-year increases in average monthly SNAP benefits.
 The findings come from SmartAsset’s new report, “SNAP Reliance and Benefits by State – 2026 Study.” 
 Overall, the study ranked Minnesota 46th nationally for the smallest decline in SNAP beneficiaries, with enrollment dropping just 4% year over year. The slight decline comes despite expanded work requirements mandated by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025.
 “SNAP enrollment has declined substantially, but the magnitude varies, ranging from a massive 54% drop in Arizona to more modest declines in some Upper Midwest states,” SmartAsset researcher Toby Nelson told The Center Square in an exclusive interview. “We estimate that approximately one in thirteen Minnesotans were receiving SNAP benefits in 2026, with an average monthly benefit of $163.35 per person.”
 Arizona recorded the largest decline in SNAP beneficiaries at 54%. Only Hawaii, New Hampshire and Alaska reported smaller declines than Minnesota.
 SNAP provides food assistance to about 40 million Americans, including approximately 450,000 Minnesotans.
 A spokesperson for the Minnesota Department of Children, Youth, and Families told The Center Square that the state has been working to implement the “complex” new requirements but expressed opposition to the changes.
 “This law expands work requirements to older adults and certain families with children, shifts millions of dollars in costs to the state and local governments, and makes it harder for Minnesotans to access food,” the spokesperson said. “Despite significant delays in federal guidance from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, and cuts to federal support for SNAP administration, DCYF is proud of the hard work done in Minnesota to implement these complex federal requirements while mitigating negative impacts on Minnesotans to the extent possible.”
 The spokesperson added that the “full impact of the new policies on SNAP participants” will continue into 2027.
 The study comes amid a recent Center Square investigation that found Minnesota and the U.S. Department of Agriculture disagree over the scope of a SNAP waiver the state is currently applying statewide. Minnesota also faces continued scrutiny over widespread fraud concerns involving taxpayer-funded welfare programs and questions about oversight and accountability.
 Against that backdrop, The Center Square asked the USDA about the study’s findings and whether the agency believes Minnesota has adequately implemented the expanded SNAP work requirements.
 “Broad-based categorical eligibility has bloated the welfare rolls for decades,” a spokesperson told The Center Square. “It has allowed states like Minnesota to take short cuts, balloon error rates, and provide benefits to those with income and assets far above federal limits, benefits meant for the neediest among us.”
 The USDA also flagged concerns over a lack of asset or income requirements for SNAP recipients in Minnesota.
 “In Minnesota, the State has completely eliminated asset limits and allowed individuals to be within 200% of the federal poverty level. And this happens through every household, regardless of circumstance,” the spokesperson said. “This means households could have significant assets, and gross incomes anywhere between $31,920 - $179,600 dependent on household size and still receive taxpayer-funded food stamp benefits. Correcting this loophole is long overdue. And in Minnesota, this is not a new loophole.”
 A separate study ranked Minnesota third nationally for the highest average monthly SNAP benefit per person, at $258.
 The 50-state study , conducted by Single Mothers Grants, analyzed data from 2021 through 2025, accounting for the discrepancy between its findings and SmartAsset’s averages. Only Hawaii and Alaska ranked higher.
 “That ranking is driven largely by the pandemic years,” a spokesperson for Single Mothers Grants told The Center Square in an exclusive interview. “Minnesota kept emergency allotments until early 2023, and benefits averaged $366 per person in 2021 and $346 in 2022. Once those allotments ended, benefits fell.”
 The SmartAsset study also found that Minnesota recorded a 2.9% year-over-year increase in average monthly benefits, the second-largest increase nationwide.
 “This could reflect several factors, including cost-of-living adjustments, changes in household income and the composition of SNAP recipients,” Nelson said. “For instance, if recipients receiving smaller benefits leave the program, the statewide average can rise even without an increase in benefits for those who remain.”
 The Minnesota DCYF spokesperson emphasized that the state does not determine SNAP benefit increases.
 “Currently, SNAP benefits are funded by the federal government, and the state does not control increases to SNAP benefit levels,” the spokesperson said. “The USDA adjusts SNAP benefit levels, known as maximum allotments, at the beginning of each federal fiscal year in accordance with federal law. These annual adjustments are calculated by USDA to reflect changes in the cost of living.”
 Expanded work requirements are not the only changes coming to SNAP. Beginning in federal fiscal year 2028, states will also be required to cover a portion of SNAP benefit costs. The spokesperson expressed concern about the additional financial responsibility.
 “This new benefit cost-sharing requirement, passed by Congress under the One Big Beautiful Bill, will shift millions of dollars in new costs onto the state and local governments,” the spokesperson said. “It is likely some states will not be able to afford this unprecedented and substantial cost shift. Minnesota faces hard budgetary choices ahead to ensure our state can continue to participate in SNAP so Minnesotans in need get help feeding themselves and their children.”
 Elyse Apel, a graduate of Hillsdale College, is a reporter for The Center Square covering Minnesota and Michigan. Her work has appeared in a range of national outlets, including the Washington Examiner , The American Spectator , and The Daily Wire .
